title: A Home with Doors
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The bridge reopened without a ribbon.

That was Toph's condition.

"No speeches until somebody actually walks across it," she said.

Danse looked at the inspection report.

"Agreed."

Aang smiled.

"I was going to suggest a small ceremony."

"Of course you were."

Katara folded her arms.

"Could we focus on the bridge?"

The repair crew had replaced the weakened support and tested the ramp after two storms. Edda had checked the grade, turning space, traction, and handrail height. Sela had reviewed the revised drainage route, confirming that water now moved away from her garden instead of collecting against the wall. The cart drivers had tested their loads.

There was no one heroic signature at the bottom.

There were many names.

Tamsin read the final report aloud because the people who had done the work deserved to hear what had passed and what still needed maintenance. The bridge was safe for the listed loads. Heavy carts would continue using the ridge until the next inspection. The old lower service passage remained sealed.

That was the agreement.

Edda approached the ramp first.

No one carried her. No one turned the crossing into a demonstration of someone's generosity. She moved at her own pace, stopped to test the handrail, and continued across.

At the far side she turned.

"Works," she said.

Toph grinned.

"Now we can have the speech."

We laughed.

There was no speech.

There was tea and bread, the sound of carts moving along the safer path, and a handful of children racing one another until Katara reminded them not to run into the people still crossing.

I stood beside the railing and watched the neighborhood come back to life.

Aang slipped his hand into mine.

"Happy?" he asked.

"Relieved."

"That's a kind of happy."

"Today it is."

He leaned against me.

The bridge had been a long argument. It had cost money, slowed deliveries, and forced people to admit that the original plan had overlooked those who used it. It would need maintenance again. Nothing about reopening made the past disappear.

But people could cross.

That was enough.

By evening our house was full of guests.

Mara had brought bread. Iroh arrived with tea. Greg was helping Pip hang a small set of lanterns near the garden gate. Maui came carrying a crate of vegetables and an expression of triumph until Toph made him put it down and wash his hands.

Severus appeared briefly with a copy of the updated maintenance records for Aang, then looked as though he regretted allowing so many people to see him.

Danse inspected the back step while pretending he was merely passing through.

I watched the people I cared about fill the rooms.

It would have been easy to make the evening into an enormous declaration that we had finally built a perfect home.

We hadn't.

We had built a place where people were allowed to disagree, leave, visit, and come back.

Katara found me by the doorway.

"You've been standing here for a while," she said.

"Taking it in."

"Anything wrong?"

"No."

She smiled.

"Then come eat."

We sat together at the table, though not everyone could fit at once. People took turns. Toph complained that the chairs were too close to the wall. Greg moved one without being asked to do everything else. Iroh poured tea for those who wanted it, then sat down to drink his own.

Maui told a story about a heroic fish, with only a modest amount of exaggeration.

Severus disputed one detail.

The argument was magnificent.

I laughed until my face hurt.

After the guests left, the house returned to its ordinary size.

Aang washed the dishes. Toph swept the floor in a way that made it clear she considered the task an insult to her talents. Katara opened the windows to let the warm air out.

I stood by the bedroom door with my green notebook in my hands.

Katara noticed.

"Writing?"

"Maybe."

She came beside me.

"About what?"

"Doors."

She looked confused.

I smiled.

"When I first came here, I thought finding a home meant knowing where I had to stay. Now I think it means knowing I can leave and still be welcome."

Katara took my hand.

"That's a good thing to know."

Aang joined us.

"Are you going somewhere?"

"Not tonight."

Toph appeared in the doorway.

"Then stop making a dramatic speech about it and come sit down."

I laughed.

We sat together in the living room, each with our own place and no need to make the arrangement identical every night.

Aang rested his head against Katara's shoulder. Toph leaned against my side. I felt the quiet warmth of their presence and the strange relief of not needing to turn it into a permanent promise of sameness.

"Can I ask something?" I said.

Toph groaned.

"Here comes the meeting."

"No meeting."

"Good."

"Are we happy with the way we're doing this?"

There was a pause.

Aang smiled.

"Today? Yes."

Katara nodded.

"Yes. And if something changes, we talk."

Toph squeezed my hand.

"Obviously."

I looked at each of them.

"Good."

Later I took the small key to my room from the hook by the door. It opened a place that belonged to me, not as a secret from the others but as a right I didn't have to earn.

I placed it beside the green notebook.

The house had doors to the garden, the street, the Threadway, and the rooms where we slept. None of them existed to trap us inside.

In the morning, I woke to the sound of Toph arguing with the kettle.

Aang was making breakfast. Katara was reading a letter from the South.

The bridge was open, the village was working, and the people I loved were already finding new things to disagree about.

I smiled.

Home, I decided, sounded exactly like that.
